Welcome back. Three weeks is a long time between sessions, so expect today to feel rusty for the first hour. That's normal. The refresher section (§1) is designed for exactly that.

Today's focus is the two statistical methods that are standard in modern corpus linguistics and sociolinguistics:

- **Mixed-effects regression** — the inferential workhorse when your data is grouped (observations within speakers, within texts, within items)
- **Conditional inference trees** — a complementary method for exploring interactions and visualising subgroup patterns

By the end of the day you'll have:

- Fit a linear mixed-effects model and interpreted its output
- Fit a logistic mixed-effects model with random intercepts
- Fit a conditional inference tree and produced a publication-quality version

Honest framing: you will not master mixed-effects models in one day. You WILL leave able to fit, interpret, and report one. That's enough to use them in your Prüfungsleistung.

## Before we start

Packages needed today:

```{r install-day3, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c(
  "lme4", "lmerTest", "performance", "MuMIn", "sjPlot",
  "partykit", "ggparty", "broom"
))
```

Load everything:

```{r load-day3}
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(performance)
library(sjPlot)
library(partykit)
library(ggparty)
library(dplyr)
```

Data files needed in your `data/` folder:

- `mbd.rda` — speech-unit-final discourse *like* in Irish English (loads as `mblrdata`)

We'll also use `sleepstudy` for the linear mixed-effects example — that one is built into the `lme4` package, no download needed.

## §1. Refresher — statistics and regression concepts

Fifty minutes. The goal is that you can read an `lm()` output confidently before we move to mixed-effects models.

### What a regression tells you

A regression model describes how one variable (the **outcome**) depends on one or more others (**predictors**). Linear regression predicts a continuous outcome; logistic regression predicts a binary one.

For a simple linear regression `lm(y ~ x)`:

- **Intercept** = predicted y when x = 0
- **Slope of x** = change in y per unit change in x
- **Standard error** = uncertainty around the coefficient
- **p-value** = probability of seeing a coefficient this large if the true coefficient were zero
- **R²** = proportion of variance in y explained by the model

### Try it with a built-in dataset

```{r refresh-mtcars}
m1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
summary(m1)
```

Read the output:

- The `wt` coefficient is around -5.3 — "each 1000-lb increase in weight is associated with 5.3 fewer miles per gallon"
- The p-value is tiny — strong evidence against "no relationship"
- Multiple R² is around 0.75 — weight explains three-quarters of the variance in mpg

### Tidy outputs

`broom` gives you the coefficient table as a tibble, which is easier to use programmatically:

```{r refresh-broom}
broom::tidy(m1)
broom::glance(m1)
```

### Visualise

```{r refresh-plot}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon",
       title = "mpg ~ wt") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Multiple predictors

Add a second predictor:

```{r refresh-multi}
m2 <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
summary(m2)
```

The `wt` coefficient changed from the single-predictor model. That's because each coefficient is "the effect of this predictor **holding others constant**". Controlling for `hp`, the apparent effect of `wt` is smaller.

### No exercise — this is a refresher

Move on when you can read the `summary()` output without having to look things up.

---

## §2. Linear mixed-effects models

105 minutes. The goal is to fit a linear mixed-effects model, understand random intercepts and random slopes, and interpret the output.

### Why mixed-effects

Most real data is grouped. Subjects produce multiple tokens. Speakers come from multiple corpora. Students belong to multiple schools. Fitting a plain `lm()` on grouped data violates **independence of observations** — a fundamental assumption.

The mixed-effects solution: treat the grouping variable (Subject, Speaker, Item) as a **random effect**. You estimate the variability among groups, not each group's intercept individually. Fewer parameters, more generalisable results.

- **Random intercepts** — each group gets its own baseline. All groups share the same slope.
- **Random slopes** — each group gets its own baseline AND its own slope for a predictor.

### The sleepstudy dataset

`sleepstudy` is the canonical teaching example: 18 subjects, 10 days of sleep deprivation per subject, reaction time as the outcome.

```{r sleep-inspect}
head(sleepstudy)
summary(sleepstudy)
```

### What goes wrong if you ignore grouping

```{r sleep-wrong}
m_wrong <- lm(Reaction ~ Days, data = sleepstudy)
summary(m_wrong)
```

The Days coefficient tells you reaction time slows by ~10ms per day. But this ignores that each subject has their own baseline and might slow down at a different rate. The standard errors are also wrong — all observations within a subject are correlated.

### Random intercept model

```{r sleep-intercept}
m1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
summary(m1)
```

Read the output top to bottom:

- **Random effects** block: `sd(Intercept) = 37.1` — the standard deviation of subject intercepts. Subjects differ by about 37ms in their baseline reaction time.
- **Residual** sd: 30.9 — the within-subject variability
- **Fixed effects** block: the `Days` coefficient is ~10.47ms per day

The `(1 | Subject)` syntax means "random intercept for Subject". The `1` is the intercept; the `|` separates random effects from grouping variable.

### Random intercept AND random slope

Allow each subject to have their own rate of slowing:

```{r sleep-slope}
m2 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)
summary(m2)
```

The Random effects block now has two variances AND a correlation between intercepts and slopes. The `Days` coefficient is similar, but we've captured the fact that subjects differ in both WHERE they start and HOW FAST they slow down.

### Compare the two models

```{r sleep-compare}
anova(m1, m2)
AIC(m1, m2)
```

The likelihood ratio test and the AIC both prefer the random-slopes model (lower AIC). The additional variance component is justified.

### Visualise individual subject slopes

```{r sleep-viz}
ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(x = Days, y = Reaction, group = Subject)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(stat = "smooth", method = "lm", se = FALSE,
            alpha = 0.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm",
              se = FALSE, colour = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual subject slopes (blue) vs population slope (red)",
    x     = "Days of sleep deprivation",
    y     = "Reaction time (ms)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Each blue line is one subject. The red line is the population average. The spread of blue lines shows the subject variability captured by the random slopes.

### Diagnostics in one line

```{r sleep-diagnostics}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

performance::check_model(
  m2,
  check = c("qq", "homogeneity", "linearity", "reqq")
)
```

This gives you residual plots, normality checks, collinearity, and influential-observation checks in one call.

### Publication-ready model summary

```{r sleep-tabmodel}
sjPlot::tab_model(m2)
```

### Marginal and conditional R²

```{r sleep-r2}
performance::r2(m2)
```

- **Marginal R²** — variance explained by fixed effects alone
- **Conditional R²** — variance explained by fixed + random effects

## §3. Logistic mixed-effects models

Seventy-five minutes. The goal is to fit a logistic mixed-effects model and interpret the output in odds ratios.

### When to go logistic

Your outcome is binary: present/absent, used/not-used, correct/incorrect. A linear model is wrong for binary outcomes — predictions can fall outside [0, 1] and residuals are not normal.

**Logistic regression** models the LOG-ODDS of the outcome. `glmer()` with `family = binomial` fits the mixed version.

### Loading the data

The dataset is 2,000 observations of speech-unit-final discourse *like* in Irish English:

```{r load-mblr}
mblrdata <- readRDS(here::here("data", "mbd.rda"))
glimpse(mblrdata)
```

What you have:

- `ID` — speaker ID (grouping variable)
- `Age` — speaker age (categorical)
- `Gender` — speaker gender
- `ConversationType` — mixed-gender or same-gender conversation
- `Priming` — whether a preceding *like* was present
- `SUFlike` — the outcome: 1 = like appears, 0 = does not

### Fit a simple logistic MEM

```{r log-fit}
m_log <- glmer(
  SUFlike ~ Priming + (1 | ID),
  data   = mblrdata,
  family = binomial
)

summary(m_log)
```

### Why log-odds are confusing — exponentiate

The coefficient for `PrimingPrime` is in log-odds space. That's not intuitive. Exponentiate to get odds ratios:

```{r log-odds}
exp(fixef(m_log))
```

An odds ratio of ~3.0 for priming means: "when the preceding context has a like, the odds of SUFlike are roughly 3× higher than when it doesn't."

### Publication-ready summary

```{r log-tab}
sjPlot::tab_model(m_log)
```

### Visualise predicted probabilities

Log-odds are abstract. Predicted probabilities are concrete:

```{r log-plot}
sjPlot::plot_model(m_log, type = "pred", terms = "Priming")
```

### Add a second predictor

```{r log-fit2}
m_log2 <- glmer(
  SUFlike ~ Priming + Gender + (1 | ID),
  data   = mblrdata,
  family = binomial
)

summary(m_log2)
sjPlot::tab_model(m_log2)
```

### Convergence warnings

Logistic MEMs are fragile. You may see warnings like `boundary (singular) fit` or `Model failed to converge`. Standard remedies:

1. Simplify the random effects structure (drop random slopes, keep only intercepts)
2. Centre numeric predictors
3. Switch optimisers: `control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")`

### Exercise 3.1 — fit and interpret

Fill in the gaps to fit a model with two predictors and extract odds ratios.

```{r ex-3-1, eval=FALSE}

)

# Extract odds ratios

```

## §4. Conditional inference trees

Sixty minutes. The goal is to fit a CIT, interpret the plot, and produce a publication-quality version.

### What CITs add to regression

Mixed-effects regression quantifies direction and magnitude. CITs find and visualise interactions. They complement regression; they do not replace it.

**Conditional inference trees** use permutation tests at each internal node to decide whether to split and on which variable. Only predictors with real statistical evidence appear in the tree. Default significance threshold: α = .05.

### Fit a CIT on the same data

Since CITs do classification on a factor, we convert `SUFlike` to a factor first:

```{r cit-prep}
citdata <- mblrdata |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(where(is.character), as.factor),
    SUFlike = as.factor(SUFlike)
  )

str(citdata)
```

Fit:

```{r cit-fit}
set.seed(111)
cit1 <- ctree(SUFlike ~ Age + Gender + ConversationType + Priming,
              data = citdata)
```

The `set.seed()` call makes the result reproducible — CITs can be sensitive to tie-breaking in the permutation tests.

### Plot the basic tree

```{r cit-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
plot(cit1)
```

### Reading the plot

- **Internal nodes** show the splitting variable and a p-value
- **Edge labels** show the values that route observations down each branch
- **Leaf nodes** show the outcome distribution in that subgroup as a bar chart
- The taller bar at a leaf is the predicted class

### Programmatic access

For reporting in your Quarto document, pull values from the fitted object rather than retyping from the plot:

```{r cit-access}
all_nodes <- nodeids(cit1)
terminal_nodes <- nodeids(cit1, terminal = TRUE)

cat("Total nodes:    ", length(all_nodes), "\n")
cat("Leaf nodes:     ", length(terminal_nodes), "\n")

# p-values at internal nodes
pvals <- unlist(nodeapply(
  cit1,
  ids = all_nodes,
  FUN = function(n) info_node(n)$p.value
))

pvals[!is.na(pvals) & pvals < .05]
```

### Adjusting the significance threshold

A stricter α produces a simpler tree:

```{r cit-strict, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
cit_strict <- ctree(
  SUFlike ~ Age + Gender + ConversationType + Priming,
  data    = citdata,
  control = ctree_control(alpha = 0.01)
)

plot(cit_strict)
```

**Important:** set α before fitting, not after seeing the tree. Post-hoc α tightening is a researcher-degrees-of-freedom problem.

### Publication-quality version with ggparty

```{r cit-ggparty, fig.width=11, fig.height=7}
set.seed(111)
cit1 <- ctree(SUFlike ~ Age + Gender + ConversationType + Priming,
              data = citdata)

pvals <- unlist(nodeapply(
  cit1,
  ids = nodeids(cit1),
  FUN = function(n) info_node(n)$p.value
))

ggparty(cit1) +
  geom_edge() +
  geom_edge_label() +
  geom_node_label(
    line_list = list(
      aes(label = splitvar),
      aes(label = paste0(
        "N = ", nodesize,
        ", p ",
        ifelse(pvals < .001, "< .001",
               paste0("= ", round(pvals, 3)))
      ))
    ),
    line_gpar = list(list(size = 13), list(size = 10)),
    ids = "inner"
  ) +
  geom_node_label(
    aes(label = paste0("Node ", id, "\nN = ", nodesize)),
    ids = "terminal",
    nudge_y = -0.01
  ) +
  geom_node_plot(
    gglist = list(
      geom_bar(aes(x = "", fill = SUFlike),
               position = position_fill(),
               color = "black"),
      theme_minimal(),
      scale_fill_manual(values = c("gray50", "gray80"),
                        guide = "none"),
      scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1)),
      xlab(""),
      ylab("Probability")
    ),
    shared_axis_labels = TRUE
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Conditional inference tree: SUFlike",
    subtitle = "Predictors: Age, Gender, ConversationType, Priming"
  )
```

# Solutions

## Solution 2.1 — linear MEM

```{r sol-2-1}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
# Random intercept only
my_m1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), data = sleepstudy)

# Random intercept AND slope
my_m2 <- lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject), data = sleepstudy)

# Compare
anova(my_m1, my_m2)

# Diagnostics on the winning model
# (subset of checks — the full panel needs a very large Plots window)
performance::check_model(
  my_m2,
  check = c("qq", "homogeneity", "linearity", "reqq")
)

# Publication-ready summary
sjPlot::tab_model(my_m2)
```

**What to look for:** `anova(my_m1, my_m2)` returns a likelihood ratio test; the p-value is tiny, so the random-slopes model is preferred. The `check_model()` output shows residuals looking reasonable, normality holding, no collinearity (only one predictor). The `tab_model()` output is the format you'd put into a Methods/Results section of your Prüfungsleistung.

## Solution 3.1 — logistic MEM

```{r sol-3-1}
my_log <- glmer(
  SUFlike ~ Priming + ConversationType + (1 | ID),
  data   = mblrdata,
  family = binomial
)

summary(my_log)

# Odds ratios
exp(fixef(my_log))

# Publication table
sjPlot::tab_model(my_log)

# Predicted probabilities for ConversationType
sjPlot::plot_model(my_log, type = "pred", terms = "ConversationType")
```

**What to look for:** The odds ratios tell you how the odds of SUFlike change for each predictor level. Priming's odds ratio should be well above 1 — strong effect. ConversationType's odds ratio tells you whether same-gender vs mixed-gender conversations affect SUFlike use. The plot makes this concrete: predicted probability on the y-axis is easier to interpret than log-odds.

## Solution 4.1 — CIT

```{r sol-4-1, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
set.seed(111)
my_cit <- ctree(
  SUFlike ~ Age + Gender + ConversationType + Priming,
  data = citdata
)

plot(my_cit)

pvals <- unlist(nodeapply(
  my_cit,
  ids = nodeids(my_cit),
  FUN = function(n) info_node(n)$p.value
))
pvals[!is.na(pvals) & pvals < .05]

dir.create(here::here("figures"), showWarnings = FALSE)
png(here::here("figures", "my_cit.png"),
    width = 10, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(my_cit)
dev.off()
```

**What to look for:** The tree shows which predictors differentiated SUFlike usage significantly. The root node is the most important predictor (smallest adjusted p-value). The leaf bar charts show the SUFlike probability in each subgroup. Compare the tree's picture to your logistic MEM's coefficients — do they tell the same story?
